chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from some of our companions, from Ali ibn Uqbah ibn Qays ibn Sam'an ibn Abu Rabiha, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), who raised it (to the Prophet or Imam), saying:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was asked, 'With what do you recognize your Lord?' He said, 'With what He introduced Himself.' It was said, 'How did He introduce Himself to you?' He said, 'No image resembles Him, nor is He perceived by the senses, nor comparable to people. He is Near in His Farness, and Far in His Nearness. He is Above all things, yet it cannot be said that 'something is above Him.' He is in front of all things, yet it cannot be said that 'He has a front.' He is Inside the things, but not like something inside something else. He is Outside the things, but not like something outside something else. Glory be to Him who is thus, and there is none like Him thus. He is the Originator of all things.'
ai.seo_question: How does the Imam describe the attributes of God in relation to space, form, and perception?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Tawhid elucidates the epistemological principle that divine recognition (ma'rifah) is initiated by God's self-revelation, emphasizing His absolute transcendence (tanzih) from physical form and sensory perception. It articulates the dialectic of divine immanence and transcendence, noting that while He is above all creation, He is not spatially contained within it, a concept central to Shia theological discourse on God's attributes. The narration concludes by affirming God as the unique Originator, reinforcing the monotheistic core of Surah al-Ikhlas.
